reader.title: Lynching of three men at Colorado, New Mexico
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Vigilantes seized three men accused of robbing a woman and hanged them from telegraph poles (A1, A4); the brief calls it a lynching (A2).

Three men were reported hanged by 'vigilantes' who seized them in a saloon on the night of the robbery, with no officers or court involved (A1, A4); the account frames it as summary 'justice' for robbing a woman, and the plural body of vigilantes seizing three men together implies a group of three or more, though no number is given (A4).

All reports trace to one secondhand Leadville Herald interview with an unnamed traveler (A1, A4); the wire brief carries the same pairing with the San Marcial shooting and appears condensed from it (A2), and no New Mexico report was found.

summary.text: The lynching of three men at Colorado, New Mexico, was the hanging of three unnamed men by vigilantes at the terminus of the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe railway, reported in January 1881.
The men were accused of robbing a woman and were hanged from telegraph poles the same night.
The story reached the national press through a Leadville, Colorado, newspaper interview and circulated as an example of frontier summary justice.
Colorado, N. Mex., was described as the 'present terminus' of the railway, about a mile and a half from an older settlement.
The only account came from a former Leadville resident who had just returned from the terminus and was interviewed by the Leadville Herald.
According to that interview, a woman named Mary McBride was walking from the terminus to the old town when four men surrounded her and demanded her money.
When she refused, they took $137 from her, which the account called 'the last cent she had.'
She returned to the end of the track and described the men.
That night three of the four were found playing cards in a saloon.
Vigilantes seized them "without a word," marched them out, and hanged them from the telegraph poles.
The account did not name the three men, give their race, or say how many vigilantes took part.
The interview said that the "avengers returned to their homes as if nothing unusual had occurred."
No report of an inquest, arrest or official response appears in the coverage, and the fourth man is not mentioned again.
The Chicago Tribune printed a summary of the interview on January 19, 1881, from a Leadville dispatch dated January 10, among its 'Far-West Episodes'.
The Memphis Daily Appeal ran the Herald text in full under the headline 'No Unnecessary Ceremony Over It', and the Claiborne Guardian reprinted it in February as 'No Ceremony Over It'.
The story's language favored the lynchers, saying that "justice was indeed summary" and calling the hanged men "villains" and "ruffians."
A one-sentence version, saying three men were "recently lynched" for having robbed a woman, ran in the 'Late News Items' columns of weeklies in Mississippi, Tennessee and Louisiana.
Both versions paired the hanging with the shooting of two "desperadoes" at nearby San Marcial, which suggests that the brief was condensed from the same interview.
None of the papers mentioned race, and no report from a New Mexico paper was found.

accounts.label: Leadville Herald interview with a traveler
accounts.gist: Four men robbed Mary McBride of $137; that night vigilantes found three of them playing cards in a saloon, marched them out and hanged them from telegraph poles, then went home.

accounts.label: Wire news brief
accounts.gist: Three men were recently lynched at Colorado, N. Mex., for having robbed a woman, and two desperadoes were shot at nearby San Marcial.

framing.detail: The Leadville Herald story says 'justice was indeed summary', calls the men 'villains' and 'ruffians' and the lynchers 'avengers', under the headline 'No Unnecessary Ceremony Over It'.
Southern weeklies carried a one-sentence brief in their 'Late News Items' columns without comment.
The Chicago Tribune ran the interview as one of its 'Far-West Episodes' from a Leadville dispatch.
